candidates.snippet: The right to erasure under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), also called the "right to be forgotten", allows a data subject to ask a controller to delete personal data without undue delay. It is set out in Article 17 GDPR. The right is not absolute, and mishandling it is one of the most common compliance failures that supervisory authorities identify.

candidates.title: What are the exceptions to the GDPR right to erasure?
candidates.snippet: Short answer: The right to erasure (right to be forgotten) under Article 17 is not absolute. Organisations can refuse erasure requests when the data is needed for exercising freedom of expression, legal obligation compliance, public health purposes, archiving in the public interest, or establishing, exercising, or defending legal claims.
